title: The Choir of Marrow Creek
premise: August Underhill hosts a late-night call-in show in the dying town of Marrow Creek, where twelve years ago a flood swallowed the old quarry settlement and everyone in it. When callers begin phoning in—voices August recognizes as the drowned dead—they beg the host to finish 'the song' their families sang to keep something beneath the water asleep. The excavation crew's discovery of a door sealed from the inside proves the drowned didn't drown; they were locked away by their own neighbors, and the song was a leash. As August uncovers that their own grandfather led the sealing, they must learn the final verse from the dead themselves without joining the choir, and end it at the door before the town's surviving descendants, desperate to silence the truth and the dead alike, can sing it for them.
about_author: Oscar Ravensworth is the pen name of a former small-market radio producer who spent a decade on overnight shifts in towns the maps forgot. They write horror about communities that survive by agreeing not to remember.

chapters.title: Dead Air
chapters.summary: August's POV. A routine broadcast is interrupted by a caller whose voice August recognizes as Denny Voss, drowned twelve years ago. August blames a prank or a recording, but the caller knows things only Denny knew. Emotional beat: dread disguised as professional composure.

chapters.title: The Excavation
chapters.summary: POV of Wren Okafor, foreman of the quarry drainage crew. Her team hits a stone door sealed from the inside, its hinges fused, its surface carved with a line of musical notation. She pockets a rubbing of it. Emotional beat: curiosity curdling into unease.

chapters.title: Second Caller
chapters.summary: August's POV. More calls arrive: the drowned, polite, patient, asking August to 'finish what your family started.' August digs out their grandfather's old broadcast logs and finds pages torn out. Emotional beat: denial cracking under pattern recognition.

chapters.title: What the Water Kept
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. The door resists every tool; one worker who hums near it goes missing overnight, his boots found facing the stone. Wren plays the notation rubbing on her phone and hears a hum answer through forty feet of rock. Emotional beat: rationalism failing.

chapters.title: Grandfather's Tape
chapters.summary: August's POV. In the station attic August finds a reel-to-reel: their grandfather broadcasting the sealing night in 1974, narrating as townsfolk chained the quarry folk behind the door to stop the disappearances. Emotional beat: inherited guilt, the horror of complicity.

chapters.title: The Verse We Never Learned
chapters.summary: Dual POV. August and Wren compare notes: the song has three known verses sung by the living, but the fourth exists only among the sealed. The dead callers say time runs out when the water does—the drainage project will empty the quarry in weeks. Emotional beat: reluctant alliance.

chapters.title: Choir Practice
chapters.summary: August's POV. On air, August lets a dead caller sing one line live; switchboards light up across town as dozens of listeners report hearing it in their own kitchens. The town remembers all at once. Emotional beat: the terrible intimacy of shared memory.

chapters.title: The Descendants
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. A committee of founding families, led by councilman Harlan Pike, confronts August: the sealing saved Marrow Creek, and finishing the song might free what's inside. They offer money, then threats. Emotional beat: justice versus order, both wearing ugly faces.

chapters.title: Boots Facing the Door
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Another worker vanishes; this time Wren follows humming through the drainage tunnel and finds him standing at the door, singing harmonies he never learned, eyes open underwater-dry. She drags him back; he doesn't speak again. Emotional beat: the cost of proximity.

chapters.title: Twelve Years of Explanations
chapters.summary: August's POV. Flashback chapter: the night young August heard the first noises after the flood and chose, like everyone, to explain them away. Present-day August admits the show itself may be the summons—the microphone is their grandfather's. Emotional beat: self-indictment.

chapters.title: The Fourth Verse, Partially
chapters.summary: August's POV. A dead caller—Denny—teaches August half the fourth verse over the air, warning that hearing it whole means singing it whole. August transcribes only fragments, hiding them in the station safe. Emotional beat: hunger for knowledge balanced against survival.

chapters.title: Pike's Sermon
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Harlan Pike holds a town meeting proposing to pour concrete into the tunnel and bury the door forever. Wren realizes entombment won't stop the song—it will just make the choir patient. Emotional beat: watching a community choose comfortable cruelty again.

chapters.title: Static Between Verses
chapters.summary: August's POV. The station's signal begins broadcasting on its own at 3 a.m., playing the third verse backward. Listeners sleepwalk toward the quarry. August barricades themselves in the booth and burns the grandfather's tape—but the song continues without it. Emotional beat: loss of control over one's own voice.

chapters.title: Inside Voices
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Through a hairline crack in the door, Wren hears the sealed—not screaming, but singing in rounds, sustained for twelve years. One voice asks her, gently, if she's come to apologize. Emotional beat: pity for the imprisoned, horror at what imprisonment made them.

chapters.title: The Ledger
chapters.summary: August's POV. August finds the founding families' ledger listing every person sealed, including children, including a name crossed out: someone escaped the night of the sealing. The last entry is their grandmother's handwriting. Emotional beat: inheritance revealed as debt.

chapters.title: The Escaped One
chapters.summary: Dual POV. The escaped sealee is alive: Miss Ada Rill, the town's ancient piano teacher, who has kept the fourth verse memorized and unsung for fifty years. She agrees to teach it—if August promises to use it to end the song, not free the thing it binds. Emotional beat: fragile trust between survivors.

chapters.title: Concrete Night
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Pike's crew pours concrete despite everything; the mixer jams, workers hear their own names in the aggregate, and the wet concrete dries carved with notation no one wrote. Two crew members join the sleepwalkers. Emotional beat: futility of force against the inevitable.

chapters.title: Learning It Whole
chapters.summary: August's POV. Ada teaches August the fourth verse in a soundproofed room, August mouthing the words, never voicing them. The verse isn't a spell—it's an apology, an accounting of the sealing, naming every name. To sing it is to accept the debt aloud. Emotional beat: terror and moral clarity arriving together.

chapters.title: The Town Sings First
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Pike, desperate, broadcasts the first three verses himself to bind the thing permanently to the town instead. Half of Marrow Creek sings along in their sleep. The door begins to open inward. Emotional beat: catastrophe engineered by fear.

chapters.title: Last Broadcast
chapters.summary: August's POV. August takes the air one final time and sings the fourth verse live, voice breaking on the names, apologizing to the dead and the living alike while Ada harmonizes and Wren holds the studio door against Pike's men. Emotional beat: sacrifice as testimony.

chapters.title: Silence, Sealed From the Outside
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. At the quarry, the song ends mid-round. The door swings open onto an empty chamber—only boots, arranged neatly, facing outward. The dead are released, not resurrected; the thing beneath starves unheard. Pike is found humming nothing at all. Emotional beat: exhausted, ambiguous peace.

chapters.title: Sign-Off
chapters.summary: August's POV. Weeks later, August hosts a final quiet broadcast reading the ledger's names aloud, then resigns. Wren seals the quarry properly—with a memorial, not concrete. August keeps the microphone unplugged on the desk, just in case. Emotional beat: grief, accountability, and the choice to keep listening.
